content: The findings presented are based on various studies evaluating the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults. Below is a detailed explanation of the evidence and its limitations: 1. Opioid Analgesics for Chronic Low Back Pain: A single randomized controlled trial conducted in Romania (Ionescu, 2016) assessed the effects of tramadol (100 mg/day for seven days) compared to a placebo in adults aged 20–60 years with chronic low back pain. The evidence was downgraded for inconsistency (only one study, making inconsistency unassessable) and imprecision (fewer than 100 participants in the analysis). 2. Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) for Chronic Low Back Pain: For treatment durations of ≥12 weeks, the evidence was derived from trials conducted in high-income countries. NSAIDs included naproxen, diflunisal, flurbiprofen, and indomethacin. The evidence was downgraded for inconsistency (I² > 50%) and imprecision (fewer than 200 participants in the analysis). For treatment durations of <12 weeks, three trials (Berry, 1982; Ghosh, 1981; Gurrell, 2018) were analyzed. These trials included NSAIDs such as naproxen (1,100 mg/day), diflunisal (1,000 mg/day), and flurbiprofen (300 mg/day). The evidence was downgraded due to imputation of standard deviations and inconsistency (I² = 69%). 3. Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs) for Chronic Low Back Pain: For treatment durations of ≥12 weeks, three parallel trials and one crossover trial were conducted in high-income countries. SNRIs included paroxetine (20–30 mg/day), milnacipran (up to 200 mg/day), and duloxetine (up to 120 mg/day). The evidence was downgraded for risk of bias (more than 50% of participants were from studies with high risk of bias), inconsistency (I² > 50%), and imprecision (pooled estimates crossed the null and the threshold for a large effect). For shorter treatment durations, similar findings were observed, with evidence downgraded for imprecision (fewer than 200 participants in the analysis). 4. Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs) for Chronic Low Back Pain: Two parallel trials (Atkinson, 1998; Pheasant, 1983) and one crossover trial (Schukro, 2016) evaluated TCAs such as nortriptyline (up to 100 mg/day) and amitriptyline (up to 150 mg/day). The evidence was downgraded for imprecision (fewer than 200 participants) and inconsistency (I² = 88%). 5. Psychological Well-Being and Adverse Events: Psychological well-being was assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory (0–63 scale) at six months. The evidence was rated as low certainty due to imprecision (confidence intervals included no effect and crossed the threshold for a moderate effect). Discontinuation due to adverse events was reported in some trials, with moderate certainty evidence showing a 15% absolute risk difference (range: -12% to 42%). 6. Population Subgroups: Gender and sex: Limited data were available, with the proportion of female participants ranging from 11% to 61% across trials. Race/ethnicity: No data were reported. Presence of radicular leg pain: Most trials excluded patients with radicular pain, except for one trial where 12% of participants had radicular low back pain. 7. Limitations Across Studies: Many studies were downgraded for risk of bias due to fair quality ratings in a significant proportion of trials. Imprecision was a common issue, with many analyses including fewer than 200 participants or confidence intervals crossing thresholds for clinically relevant effects. Inconsistency was noted in several analyses, with high heterogeneity (I² > 50%) and insufficient data to conduct stratified or sensitivity analyses. In summary, the evidence for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain, including opioids, NSAIDs, SNRIs, and TCAs, is limited by small sample sizes, risk of bias, and inconsistency. Further high-quality research is needed to provide more definitive guidance.
